newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: FEATURE - Zambia's ramshackle taxis fuelled by faith.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Zambia's ramshackle taxis fuelled by faith.

text.p: It's easy to flag down a taxi in Zambia -- look for the most decrepit vehicle on the road.

Of the hundreds of taxis plying their trade on the streets of the capital Lusaka every day, the great majority are creaking ruins beyond redemption. Coughing and juddering, held together by wire and patches, they seem to run on pure faith.
"If it is a wreck, then it is a taxi," a Zambian journalist said.
Taxi drivers say about 4,000 taxis, including minibuses, are registered in the country's capital.
Most should have been retired gracefully to the scrapheap several years ago but Lusaka taxi drivers say their trusty cars are a testiment to good Japanese auto-making.
The average Zambian taxi is about 15 to 20 years old and is most likely to be a Datsun -- the name under which Japanese auto giant Nissan Motor Co was known in Africa about 15 years ago.
"This is a Datsun, it is still good," said one driver.
The vehicle bore no discernible trace of shock absorbers, or for that matter, interior panelling.
A badly cracked windscreen seems to be required by law, and the only air-conditioning comes through the holes in the floor.
Some still have ignition keys but others require the hot-wiring technique familiar to car thieves.
"We call them our ramshackles," driver Jeff Mupeta said fondly.
Mupeta and colleagues in the trade blame the state of their cars on the Zambian economy which began moving away from almost three decades of socialism in 1991.
According to the World Bank, Zambia is one of the poorest countries in the world with per capita Gross Domestic Product around $350.
Mupeta said most taxi drivers in Zambia had to hand over about 30,000 kwacha ($23) each day to the owner of the car -- usually a Zambian entrepreneur who bought the "ramshackle" for about $500.
"I have to pay him 30,000 each day and then find 17,000 more for petrol (gasoline)," Mupeta said.

The average fare from one of Lusaka's hotels to the city centre is about 3,500 kwacha but this increases if the taxi driver has to wait, or has not uncommon flat tyre or mechanical breakdown. There are no meters in sight.
The result is confusion and chaos for a visitor or tourist who is expected to bargain on each fare and may have to pitch in with limited mechanical knowledge or a shove to keep the vehicle going.
Sometimes the passenger is expected to steer the taxi too when the driver needs both hands to light a cigarette.
Taxi drivers said their worst enemies were unregistered pirate taxis and Zambian police who mount regular roadblocks to check the cars' roadworthiness.
"The pirates and police are our worst problems. The pirates steal from us and the police fine us," said one.
"They fine us 180,000 kwacha for a defective tyre or indicator. Failing to put on a seatbelt (safety belt) is also 180,000 kwacha -- we are not used to driving with seatbelts," Mupeta said.
Whether wearing a safety belt would reduce Lusaka's road death toll is debatable.
At the city's Central Police Station, scores of wrecks from collisions stand abandoned. Police say at least 16 people are killed daily in Lusaka in vehicle accidents.

"Accidents happen everyday in Lusaka...people die each day," Mupeta said, but quickly reassured his passengers. "Taxi drivers always drive very carefully. We take into consideration the type of vehicles we use," he added, without irony.
